english_translation: Please come in quietly because the patient has just fallen asleep.

dialogue.shona: Ndapota huyai muchinyararire nokuti murwere achangobatwa nehope.
dialogue.english: Please come in quietly because the patient has just fallen asleep.
dialogue.literal_gloss: Ndapota [ndapota] • huyai [come! (polite/plural)] • muchinyararire [in / singular chinyararire] • nokuti [because] • murwere [in / singular rwere] • achangobatwa [achangobatwa] • nehope [and / with hope]

grammar_notes.title: Giving Commands & Polite Requests ('huyai')
grammar_notes.content: Notice the command verb 'huyai' in this sentence. In Shona, a direct command to one person (singular) is simply the verb stem ending in '-a'—for example, 'Vhara!' ('Close!'), 'Tora!' ('Take!'), or 'Huya!' ('Come!'). When speaking to more than one person, or when showing polite respect to an adult, you add '-i' to the end, changing '-a' to '-ai' (as in 'Huyai!' = 'Come!' or 'Batai!' = 'Catch/Hold!'). Adding the prefix 'chi-' (as in 'Chiuya' or 'Chigara') means 'Do it right now'.
grammar_notes.rule: Singular Command: Verb stem (-a) [Huya! / Tora!] | Polite or Plural Command: Verb stem + -i (-ai) [Huyai! / Torai!]

grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Future with '-cha-' ('achangobatwa')
grammar_notes.content: Look at 'achangobatwa' in this sentence. Whenever you want to say what 'will' happen in the future, simply place the future marker '-cha-' between the subject prefix and the verb stem. For example, 'ndichabika' means 'I will cook', 'tichasvika' means 'we will arrive', and 'mvura ichanaya' means 'the rain will fall'. Pair it with 'mangwana' ('tomorrow') to talk about tomorrow's plans!
grammar_notes.rule: Subject Prefix + -cha- + Verb Stem = Future ('will') -> Ndichaenda (I will go), Vachadzoka (They will return)

grammar_notes.title: Joining Words with 'ne-' ('and / with') in 'nehope'
grammar_notes.content: Look closely at 'nehope'. In Shona, the word for 'and' or 'with' between nouns is not a separate word—instead, the prefix 'ne-' (or 'na-' before people's names) is written attached directly to the second noun! For example, 'ne-' + 'hope' forms 'nehope'. You will see this everywhere in daily speech: 'sadza nemuriwo' ('sadza and vegetables'), 'nesimba' ('with strength'), and 'nekukasira' ('with haste / quickly').
grammar_notes.rule: ne- + Noun = and / with [Noun] (written as a single word, e.g., sadza nemuriwo = sadza and vegetables)

cultural_notes.title: Visiting the Sick ('ushanya Murwere') & Quiet Consideration
cultural_notes.content: Visiting an ill relative or neighbour ('murwere') to offer comfort is a core duty in Shona culture ('kubata maoko' / 'kutarisa murwere'), and visitors enter quietly ('muchinyararire') whenever the patient has just fallen asleep ('achangobatwa nehope').
